newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE coffee nudges up on covering, NY advance.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE coffee nudges up on covering, NY advance.

text.p: London's robusta coffee futures nudged up to close slightly higher on industry short-covering helped partly by renewed advance in New York arabica futures.
Traders said scale-up trade hedge selling stopped the market from going up much further.
"London should have been $20 higher based on New York," said one trader. "But we only managed about $9 higher."
By the close, volume leader January firmed $9 at $1,410 a tonne after a high of $1,412. The contract sailed through its previous $1,405 hurdle but faced the next resistance at $1,415.
Overall volume was 3,447 lots, with January alone accounting for 2,303 lots.
Nearby Nov/Jan and Jan/March spreads were also barely moved from the levels at Tuesday's close.
New York prices were higher by mid-session after chart-driven speculative and trade buying pushed the spot December contract through key 120.00 cent a lb resistance.
But scale-up producer selling slowed the advance through the next significant 123-cent region until after the London close.
Some traders said earlier in the day that the immediate outlook for London appeared promising on the upside if the second-month position could stay above $1,400.
"But it will be more constructive if the market clears $1,420," another said later in the day.

Immediately, the market is keeping an eye on the situation in Vietnam where heavy rains have raised the moisture content of the new robusta beans to around 20 percent, well above the usual 13 percent.
Coffee arrivals from the main growing area of Dak Lak to the main coffee port of Ho Chi Minh City have been reduced to trickles due to transportation problems.
Chartwise, analysts said a break above $1,405 basis January in London could end a bear run. This would help January to secure a higher high and a higher low.
In other news, the Association of Coffee Producing Countries will review the market at a session in Costa Rica this weekend but no major policy revisions are likely.
